ground: "You alone do we serve, and You alone do we ask for help." After three ayat that speak about God (Lord of the worlds, the All-Merciful, Owner/King of the Day of Judgment), the speakers now address Him directly. In the plural they declare that their service and obedience belong to Him only, and that the help they seek comes from Him only. The object pronoun "You" is placed first, and repeated, in both clauses.

triggers.how: the same detached object pronoun is repeated and fronted before the second verb

findings.statement: The ayah says 'we serve You and ask You for help', and by putting the detached object 'iyyāka' before each verb and repeating it, it also closes both acts off to anyone else: You and no other, for service and again for help.
findings.perceptible: The exclusion is built into the word order twice, once for each act. Help is shut off from others just as separately as service is, so neither can be split between God and another backer.

triggers.how: third-person description of the master in 1:2–4

findings.statement: The ayah says 'You', and after three ayat spoken about God in the third person, that second person is the moment the speakers turn to face the one they have been describing.
findings.perceptible: The turn has a direction in space. Up to 1:4 the speakers stand describing their owner and king to no one in particular; at 1:5 they turn toward him and speak to his face. The surah's addressee changes right here.

Tahdhib glosses ʿābidūn (23:47) as dāʾinūn: 'everyone who submits to a king (dāna li-malik) is his ʿābid'. This puts ʿibāda and dīn side by side in the dictionary itself.

findings.statement: 'We serve You' names worship, and its root's noun ʿabd, the owned one who is the opposite of free, lets it also be heard as the household's owned ones telling their owner and king whose they are.
findings.perceptible: It completes the household scene of 1:2–4 (owner, king, dominion). The Turkish word ibadet points to acts done at set times. Here it becomes a standing condition of the whole person: belonging to someone and obeying him, with the Day of dīn (1:4) as the day on which that belonging is settled.

triggers.how: al-ʿAyn and Maqāyīs: 'ʿabada yaʿbudu ʿibādatan is said only of one who serves God; of a slave serving his master one does not say yaʿbuduhu'

findings.statement: 'We serve You' uses the verb that, the lexicographers say, is not used for a slave serving a human master, while the noun of the same root is the slave himself. The owned one's name and a service no human owner can claim are heard in one word.
findings.perceptible: The word itself draws the line between belonging to God and belonging to a human master. The speakers take the slave's name and give the service it implies to the one master for whom the lexicon keeps the verb.

findings.statement: 'We serve You' is humble lowering, and the same root also names the toughness and endurance of a closely woven cloth, so the lowering can be heard as something that holds.
findings.perceptible: The root joins opposites into one concept: lowered like trodden ground, and firm like tough cloth that lasts. For a reader who hears only weakness in 'kul', service here is also where the speakers get their firmness.

findings.statement: 'You alone we serve' is lowering before God, and because the root's ʿabad also means proud disdain (anafa), the 'alone' can be heard as a refusal to be lowered before anyone else.
findings.perceptible: Exclusive service carries a matching pride. The one who lowers himself before one master stands upright before all others, so 'kulluk' here is not general meekness.

findings.statement: 'We serve You' is humble service, and the root's image, which Ibn Durayd calls its origin, is a road beaten smooth by many feet. So the servant's lowering is heard in the same root as the trodden road the next ayah asks to be guided on.
findings.perceptible: It links 1:5 and 1:6–7 through a physical image. Service means being smoothed and made walkable, the way a path is. The request that follows is for a path already smoothed by the feet of those who were favored, so the servant's posture and the road share one shape.

findings.statement: 'We ask You for help' is a request for aid, and next to the ʿ-b-d branch for the traveler whose mount has given out, it can be heard as a stranded walker asking for someone to lean on.
findings.perceptible: It makes the request bodily. The one asking cannot go on alone and asks to be held up. The next ayah, whose root also names walking while supported between two people, keeps that same body upright on the road.

triggers.how: al-ʿAyn / Tahdhib (al-Layth), defining ʿawn: 'everything you seek help from or that helps you is your ʿawn, as fasting is ʿawn toward worship (al-ṣawm ʿawn ʿalā al-ʿibāda)'. The dictionary's own example joins the two roots of this ayah.
Ṣiḥāḥ: al-ʿawn = al-ẓahīr ʿalā al-amr, the backer in an undertaking; istafʿala = asking for it; Mufradāt: muʿāwana = muẓāhara (backing)

findings.statement: 'We ask You for help' is a general request for aid, and because ʿawn is backing given to someone in an undertaking ('ʿalā al-amr'), it can also be heard as asking for backing in the very service just declared.
findings.perceptible: It explains the order of the two clauses. The speakers do not hand their task over; they take it on ('we serve') and ask for someone at their back while they do it. Ẓahīr is the one who stands at your back, and that is the body of the help asked for.

findings.statement: 'We ask You for help' is a request for aid, and the root's other branches (strength catching up with years, a second war harder than the first) let the help be heard as what brings the asker's strength up to the task.
findings.perceptible: The help adds to effort rather than replacing it: it is strength that closes the gap between what one must do and what one can do. That keeps both clauses of the ayah in force at once.

findings.statement: 'You alone we serve' is worship, and because the root also names being enslaved (taʿbīd, istiʿbād) by kings and tyrants, the 'alone' can be heard as refusing every other master.
findings.perceptible: Service to God is the one servitude that shuts out all the others. The only other Quranic use of the imperative 'seek help from God' is spoken to a people enslaved by Pharaoh, which puts this ayah's two verbs side by side under an oppressor.

triggers.how: a first-person form directed at God, as in the dominant group of uses

findings.statement: 'We serve You' belongs to the Quran's recurring use of ʿabada to name whom a person gives their obedience to, often set against 'what others serve' (min dūni…).
findings.perceptible: In the Quran the verb is a choice of master: there is always an implied 'and not them'. Here 'iyyāka' makes that contrast explicit.

triggers.how: the other three uses (2:45, 2:153, 7:128) all pair seeking help with patience, prayer, or God, under pressure

findings.statement: 'We ask You for help' belongs to the Quran's few uses of istaʿāna, all of which ask for help to hold out in a trial (with patience and prayer, or with God against Pharaoh).
findings.perceptible: The help asked for is endurance under a load, not a one-time favor. It is the strength needed to keep going.

loaded_words.role: Names whom a person gives their obedience and lowering to. It is usually a contrastive choice of master (God against idols, al-ṭāghūt, Satan, what the forefathers served).
loaded_words.count: 64 of 122 uses target God, named or addressed; the other 58 name or ask about other objects of service, which keeps the contrastive role active throughout
loaded_words.departure: Turkish 'ibadet etmek' / 'tapmak' hear ritual acts or cultic worship. Here the Quranic role is choosing and naming one's master, and iyyāka sharpens it into exclusion. 'Kulluk ederiz' comes closer, but still loses the obedience and the rejection of other masters.

loaded_words.role: Seeking backing to hold out under pressure: 'seek help with patience and prayer' (2:45, 2:153) and 'seek help from God and be patient', said to the people enslaved by Pharaoh (7:128)
loaded_words.count: 4 of 4 uses keep it: every use is a request for help that goes together with endurance in a trial
loaded_words.departure: Turkish 'yardım dileriz' hears a general request for aid. The Quranic role is backing in a hard, continuing task, and ʿawn is help given 'ʿalā al-amr', on something the asker is already doing.

losses.loses: The ʿabd, the owned one and the opposite of free. The obedience of one who belongs to someone. The dīn/ʿābid equivalence (submitting to a king). The road trodden smooth that the lexicographers give as the root's origin. The paired strength (ʿabada) and disdain toward other masters (ʿabad).
losses.adds: A narrowing to ritual acts done at set times (namaz, oruç), so that 'ibadet' feels like one part of life rather than the whole person's standing.

losses.loses: The link to obedience in dīn and to the smoothed road; also the root's strength and disdain facets. The Turkish word is Turkic and does not share the Arabic root, so the root's other branches are out of reach.
losses.adds: Keeps the servant/slave sense well, but can sound like meek subservience with no matching refusal of other masters.

losses.loses: The ownership and obedience frame; the whole-person service.
losses.adds: Cultic, often idol-related connotations of adoration, and a physical rite before an object.

losses.loses: Mabet has narrowed to a building (card), abid to an ascetic devotee, ubudiyet to an abstract theological term. None of them lets the reader hear the owned one or the beaten road.
losses.adds: A sense of specialized religious space or elite piety, where the Arabic verb is said by every believer in every recitation.

losses.loses: The istafʿala 'seeking'. ʿAwn as ẓahīr, the backer at one's back in an undertaking. Muẓāhara as taking one's side. The link to endurance in the other Quranic uses.
losses.adds: A general, possibly passive request for help, as if the task were handed over.

losses.loses: Muavin is now a job title (assistant, bus attendant, per the card); iane has become a donation or collection; teavün is archaic. None carries 'seeking backing'.
losses.adds: Associations with a subordinate helper or with charity collection, which reverses the direction: here the asker is the weaker party and God the backer.

grammar: Iyyāka is a detached object pronoun placed before the verb. Fronting it restricts the act (You and no other), and repeating it applies that restriction to service and to help separately.
Iltifāt: after 1:2–4 speak of God in the third person, 1:5 switches to 'You'. The speakers turn to address him directly.
Nastaʿīn is form X (istafʿala) of ʿ-w-n, the form of seeking: 'we seek backing', not 'You help us'.
Both verbs are first person plural, so one reciter speaks as a member of a group.
reread: The owned ones of the household described in 1:2–4 turn to face their owner and king and speak to him: You and no other do we serve, You and no other do we ask to back us. Their service is lowering of the kind a road undergoes under many feet, and the root that says it also says toughness that lasts and a proud refusal to bow to any other master, including the Pharaohs who make slaves of people. The help they ask for is not a handing-over of the task but backing in the very service they have just declared: someone at their back, strength brought up to the load, as a traveler whose mount has given out leans on those beside him. From that posture the next ayah follows naturally. Lowered and held up, they ask to be led onto the road already beaten smooth by those who were favored.
